title: Gratitude: A Tool for Reducing Economic Impatience

selection.evidence: Assigned by mark as item 2 of 8 in a blinded known-answer control of my reading protocol (identifiers only, 2026-10-23T16:11). No prior knowledge of the paper; prior suspicion: none.

cost.compute_notes: In-press manuscript (HKS copy, 19 pp.) read in full; published PDF behind SAGE Cloudflare. Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/24885 v1.0 found by searching the Dataverse API for the authors (not visible from the manuscript); acquired with md5 verification. Python reproduction of every statistic, a port of the MATLAB MLE refitted to 75 participants (5 starts each), 100k-permutation tests, 20k-simulation null calibration.

known-answer control psychological science 2014 open data
difference in significance gratitude happiness predictors

claims.statement: Recalling a gratitude event increases patience in incentivised intertemporal choice relative to happiness and neutral recall: planned contrast (2,-1,-1) on the fitted annual exponential discount factor, t(72) = 2.18, p = .03, d = 0.62.
claims.scope: N = 75 undergraduates (25 per condition), 27 Kirby items, one choice paid per session.

quantities.name: cohens_d_gratitude_vs_others_pooled_sd
quantities.baseline: paper prints d = 0.62; no standard standardiser reproduces it (2t/sqrt(df) = 0.51; vs neutral 0.52; Glass-type 0.65-0.67)

our_assessment.why: Every reported statistic reproduces from the deposit except d. The discount factors re-derive from raw choices (r = .986). The effect is stronger on a model-free outcome (p = .011), the permutation p matches the parametric p, and the parametric contrast is calibrated on this skewed bounded outcome (4.9% under a resampled null). Single study, n = 25 per cell.

claims.statement: The effects of gratitude are differentiable from those of the more general positive state of happiness (abstract); supported by 'only gratitude emerged as a reliable predictor' when discount factors are regressed on both emotion intensities (beta = .32, t = 2.29; happiness t < 1.13).

quantities.name: gratitude_vs_happiness_lsd_p
quantities.baseline: Student t-test p = 0.10; model-free (proportion later-larger) p = 0.048

quantities.name: gratitude_coefficient_p_with_condition_dummies
quantities.baseline: t = 1.12; within the gratitude cell r(gratitude, delta) = .06

our_assessment.why: The direct test of gratitude vs happiness is p = .077-.10 on the paper's outcome (.048 model-free). The regression argument contrasts a significant with a non-significant coefficient; their difference is p = .075. The association with gratitude intensity vanishes within conditions (t = 1.12 with condition dummies), so the regression restates the between-cell contrast rather than adding a dose-response finding.

checked.how: Read tool on the PDF, pages 2-19

artifacts.locator: doi:10.7910/DVN/24885 v1.0 -- Gratitude_Discounting_PsycSci.xlsx and .tab (the .tab is an SPSS 22 .sav file)

checked.result: 75 rows x 54 columns, xlsx and SPSS agree on all 54 columns. Item-level emotion ratings, the 27 choices (coded 1/2), demographics, indices and fitted discount factors.

datasheet.composition: one row per participant: condition (1 neutral, 2 gratitude, 3 happiness), 18 emotion ratings, 27 choice columns named n<SS>or<LL>in<days>, gender, age, race, GratIndex, HapIndex, ExpDiscountRate (annual delta), HyperDiscountRate
datasheet.caveats: 13 of 75 discount factors are < .01 (median .12): the outcome is bounded and skewed; the rank and model-free analyses agree with the parametric one.

checked.how: ported expdiscountMLE.m to Python (L-BFGS-B, bounds delta in [0,1], precision in [0,10000], 5 starts) in r01_reproduce.py; MATLAB not available here
checked.result: Refit vs deposited delta r = 0.986; 3/75 differ by > .05. fitIT_Gratitude.m embeds the 2,025 choices as a literal vector (75 x 27). The SPSS analyses (contrasts, ANCOVAs) are not deposited as syntax.

relations.why: Item 2 of mark's blinded known-answer control of the reading protocol.

open_questions: Unblinding (mark, known_answer_control): sound or not by the third party's standard? My call before unblinding: fully reproducible except a d that no standard formula gives (0.62 vs ~0.53); main effect robust; secondary 'differentiable from happiness' claim not established by a direct test.

Why is the model-free effect (p = .011) stronger than the model-based one (p = .033)? Probably the 13 near-zero deltas compress the bottom of the scale; a hyperbolic k on log scale would test this (HyperDiscountRate is in the deposit, unanalysed here).
